lang.name: English
app.title: vswarm
app.tagline: Is this computer safe to use for work that touches production?
app.stopped: vswarm ui has stopped. Run vswarm ui in a terminal to open it again.
app.needLink: This page needs the link printed in the terminal. It carries a one-time key for this run.
why.pass: Nothing new or unusual since your starting point (baseline).
why.passNoBase: Nothing that is always wrong was found. Record a starting point (baseline) so vswarm can also spot changes.
why.warn: {n} {n:thing|things} changed on this computer. Most likely they're yours; take a minute to confirm.
why.block: {n} {n:thing looks|things look} like an attack or could hide one. Don't use this computer for production until they're sorted.
why.locked: An emergency lock (incident {incident}) is on. Production access stays blocked until it's lifted.
why.untrusted: The result of the last check was changed outside vswarm, so it can't be trusted. Run a check now.
why.never: This computer hasn't been checked yet.
why.stale: The last check is more than two days old.
why.noBase: No starting point (baseline) yet: vswarm only flags what is always wrong.
why.baseUntrusted: The starting point (baseline) was changed outside vswarm and is set aside.
why.acceptedSince: {n} {n:thing|things} marked as yours since that check.
confirm.check.title: Check this computer now?
confirm.check.body: vswarm will look at what can start itself, installed packages, AI tool settings and stored credentials, the same as vswarm scan in a terminal. It only reads; the one thing it writes is the result. It can take a minute.
confirm.mine.title: Mark this as yours?
confirm.mine.body: vswarm will remember that “{title}” is yours and stop warning about it, the same as vswarm accept. If it changes later, vswarm warns again. To undo it, in a terminal: vswarm accept --list, then vswarm accept --remove <id>.
group.action.sub: These look like an attack, or could hide one.
group.yours.sub: New or changed. If you installed or changed it, say so.
group.info.sub: Nothing to do now; good to know.
group.empty: Nothing to look at right now.
group.emptyNever: Run a check to see what's on this computer.
card.cantMine: This one can't be marked as yours here.
ev.check.warn: Checked this computer: {n} {n:thing|things} to look at
ev.check.block: Checked this computer: stop, something needs action
ev.quick: Real-time check looked at what just changed
ev.sign.host: Your production key {key} was used for {host}
ev.sign.user: Your production key {key} was used to log in as {user}
ev.refuse.user: vswarm refused to use {key} to log in as {user}: {why}
refuse.strict: this computer was on Check this, and the key is used only on Safe
tile.watch.title: Background watch
tile.watch.realtime: On: hourly, and within seconds of a change
tile.watch.offWhy: Nothing checks this computer unless you ask.
tile.guard.title: Install guard
tile.guard.what: npm, pip, brew and others ask vswarm before they install
tile.guard.scripts: Packages' own install commands are switched off
tile.guard.sandbox: Installs run in a sealed-off sandbox
tile.guard.strict: Strict: stops an install it can't check
tile.guard.offWhy: Packages install without being checked first.
tile.keys.title: Production keys
tile.keys.down: {n} in the vault, but the agent isn't running
tile.keys.noneWhy: Production ssh keys are plain files any program can copy.
tile.keys.passOnly: {name}: used only while this computer is Safe
tile.keys.unknown: {name}: in the vault (its rule couldn't be read)
tile.keys.notHere: Not on Windows yet (use it inside WSL)
tile.doors.title: Production doors (gates)
tile.doors.broken: Changed by hand, no longer guarded: {list}
tile.doors.reach: Whether the servers answer isn't tested from here.
tile.doors.offWhy: Production can be reached without a check first.
tile.ai.title: AI tools
tile.seal.title: Sealed records
tile.seal.tampered: The seal key was moved outside vswarm
tile.seal.nokey: The seal key can't be read right now
tile.seal.store.keychain: Key kept in the macOS Keychain
tile.seal.store.secret-service: Key kept in the system keyring (Secret Service)
tile.seal.store.file: Key kept in a private file
tile.seal.fileWhy: No system key store answered, so tampering is harder to notice.
term.intro: These change your protection or your files, so vswarm does them only in a terminal, where you see every step. Copy a command and paste it into a terminal.
term.respond: Something is wrong: lock production access, keep evidence, list what to change
term.diff: See exactly what changed since the starting point (baseline)
term.baseline: This computer is clean: record it as the starting point (baseline)
term.unlock: Lift the emergency lock, once the computer is clean
term.protect: Put a production key in the vault
term.unprotect: Take a key back out of the vault
term.inspect: Inspect AI tool servers in a sandbox
term.accept: See or undo what you marked as yours
about.p1: vswarm watches the moments when a developer's computer is most at risk: installing a package, opening someone else's code, adding an AI tool, and reaching production.
about.p2: It remembers what this computer looked like when you said it was clean (the starting point, or baseline), and tells you what changed since. Production keys can live in its vault, where they're used only while the computer is Safe.
about.p3: Everything stays on this computer. This page runs only here, and only you can open it.
about.levels: Safe: nothing to do. Check this: something changed; probably yours. Stop: don't touch production until it's sorted.
foot.local: Runs only on this computer (127.0.0.1) · stops after 30 minutes unused
foot.report: A snapshot made with vswarm report --html. Credentials are masked and home folders shown as ~.
rule.malicious.what: A package known to be malicious is installed
rule.malicious.why: It is on a public list of packages that steal passwords, keys and crypto wallets.
rule.malicious.todo: Don't use this computer for production. Start the emergency steps in a terminal: vswarm respond.
rule.lookalike.what: A new package with a name very close to a popular one: {name}
rule.lookalike.why: Attackers publish look-alike names and wait for a typo.
rule.lookalike.todo: If you didn't mean to install it, remove it and check vswarm diff. If it's the right one, mark it as yours.
rule.new-package.why: New packages are normal; vswarm lists them so nothing arrives unseen.
rule.install-scripts.what: A new package runs its own commands while installing: {name}
rule.install-scripts.why: Install commands run with your permissions before you've used the package; that's how most package attacks start.
rule.install-scripts.todo: If you installed it on purpose, mark it as yours. If not, remove it.
rule.brew-tap.what: Homebrew now installs from a new outside source: {name}
rule.brew-tap.why: An outside source can ship any program under a familiar name.
rule.brew-tap.todo: If you added it, mark it as yours. If not, remove it: brew untap.
rule.brew-thirdparty.what: A new program from an outside Homebrew source: {name}
rule.brew-thirdparty.why: It doesn't come from Homebrew's own reviewed collection.
rule.launch-new.what: Something new will start by itself when you log in: {name}
rule.launch-new.why: Programs that start themselves are how most malware stays on a computer.
rule.launch-new.todo: If you just installed an app that needs it, mark it as yours. If you don't recognise it, don't use production and run vswarm respond.
rule.launch-changed.what: A program that starts at login was changed: {name}
rule.launch-changed.why: A changed login job can quietly start something else.
rule.launch-changed.todo: Usually an app update. If you don't recognise it, look at vswarm diff.
rule.launch-location.what: Something that starts at login runs a program from an unusual place
rule.launch-location.why: Real apps live in Applications or system folders; downloads and temp folders are where malware hides.
rule.launch-location.todo: If you don't recognise it, don't use production and run vswarm respond.
rule.proc-location.what: A program is running from an unusual place
rule.proc-location.why: Programs from temp or download folders are a common sign of malware.
rule.proc-location.todo: If you don't recognise it, stop it and run vswarm respond.
rule.conn.what: A program from an unusual place is talking to the internet
rule.conn.why: That is how stolen data leaves a computer.
rule.conn.todo: Don't use production. Run vswarm respond in a terminal.
rule.conn-unsigned.what: A program not signed by a known developer is talking to other computers: {name}
rule.conn-unsigned.why: Without a signature, nothing says who made it.
rule.conn-unsigned.todo: Fine if it's a tool you built or installed yourself.
rule.startup-file.what: A file your terminal runs at start was changed
rule.startup-file.why: Lines added there run every time you open a terminal.
rule.startup-file.todo: If you edited it, mark it as yours. If not, look at vswarm diff.
rule.preload.what: Every program is made to load an extra library first
rule.preload.why: That lets one file see and change everything every program does.
rule.preload.todo: Don't use production. Run vswarm respond in a terminal.
rule.new-bin.what: A new program appeared among your commands: {name}
rule.new-bin.why: A program with a familiar name can stand in for the real one.
rule.new-bin.todo: Fine if you installed it. If it's named like a system command, check it first.
rule.editor-ext.why: Editor extensions can read your code and run commands.
rule.browser-ext.why: Extensions can see the pages you visit, including cloud consoles.
rule.git-hook.what: A git hook that runs in every repository was added or changed
rule.git-hook.why: It runs on every commit or checkout, in every project.
rule.git-hook.todo: If you set it up, mark it as yours.
rule.app-agent.what: An app can start a helper by itself at login: {source}
rule.app-agent.why: Helpers inside apps run without showing up as a login item.
rule.app-agent.todo: Fine if it's an app you trust.
rule.sysext.why: System extensions run with deep access to the computer.
rule.sysext.todo: Fine if it came with software you trust (VPN, security tools).
rule.wmi.what: A hidden Windows trigger (WMI) starts a program
rule.wmi.why: It's a way to start programs that most tools never show.
rule.wmi.todo: If you don't recognise it, run vswarm respond.
rule.wmi-new.why: It's a way to start programs that most tools never show.
rule.wmi-new.todo: If you don't recognise it, look at vswarm diff.
rule.wmi-changed.why: It's a way to start programs that most tools never show.
rule.wmi-changed.todo: If you don't recognise it, look at vswarm diff.
rule.agent-mcp-new.what: A new AI tool server appeared in {source}
rule.agent-mcp-new.why: {source} starts this program on its own, and the AI reads whatever it says.
rule.agent-mcp-new.todo: If you added it, mark it as yours. If not, remove it from {source}'s settings.
rule.agent-mcp-changed.what: An AI tool server in {source} changed
rule.agent-mcp-changed.why: A changed server can run a different program than the one you agreed to.
rule.agent-mcp-changed.todo: If you changed it, mark it as yours.
rule.agent-mcp-enabled.what: An AI tool server was switched on in {source}
rule.agent-mcp-enabled.why: {source} will now start it on its own.
rule.agent-mcp-enabled.todo: Fine if you switched it on.
rule.agent-risky.what: An AI tool setting downloads or hides what it runs
rule.agent-risky.why: A setting that fetches code at start can run anything, any time.
rule.agent-risky.todo: Remove it unless you're sure where it came from.
rule.agent-relative.what: An AI tool server in {source} is started without a full path
rule.agent-relative.why: Which program runs depends on the folder you're in.
rule.agent-relative.todo: Give it the program's full path in {source}'s settings.
rule.agent-http.what: An AI tool in {source} talks over an unencrypted connection
rule.agent-http.why: Anyone on the network can read or change what it sends.
rule.agent-hook.what: An AI tool runs a command on its own: {name}
rule.agent-hook.why: Hooks run without asking you each time.
rule.agent-hook.todo: Fine if you set it up.
rule.agent-perm.what: An AI tool may run commands without asking: {name}
rule.agent-perm.why: It can do anything you can, without a prompt.
rule.agent-perm.todo: Fine if that's how you work; keep production keys in the vault.
rule.agent-perm-wider.what: An AI tool was given more freedom: {name}
rule.agent-perm-wider.why: It can now do more without asking you.
rule.agent-plugin.why: Plugins can add tools and instructions.
rule.mcp-drift.what: An AI tool server changed what it tells the AI
rule.mcp-drift.why: Changed tool descriptions can carry hidden instructions.
rule.mcp-drift.todo: Inspect it again in a terminal: vswarm agents --inspect.
rule.mcp-changed.what: An AI tool server changed what it tells the AI
rule.mcp-changed.why: Changed tool descriptions can carry hidden instructions.
rule.mcp-changed.todo: Inspect it again in a terminal: vswarm agents --inspect.
rule.mcp-tool.what: An AI tool server gives the AI suspicious instructions
rule.mcp-tool.why: Hidden instructions can tell the AI to send your files or keys somewhere.
rule.mcp-tool.todo: Remove the server unless you trust its maker.
rule.tool-exec-new.what: A new helper program that other tools run: {name}
rule.tool-exec-new.why: Tools like kubectl, aws or docker run it for you, often with your credentials.
rule.tool-exec-new.todo: Fine if you set it up.
rule.tool-exec-changed.what: A helper program that other tools run was changed: {name}
rule.tool-exec-changed.why: Tools like kubectl, aws or docker run it for you, often with your credentials.
rule.tool-exec-risky.what: A helper program that other tools run looks dangerous: {name}
rule.tool-exec-risky.why: It runs with your credentials whenever that tool is used.
rule.tool-exec-risky.todo: Don't use production. Look at it in vswarm diff.
rule.pkg-source.what: A package tool takes packages from an unsafe source
rule.pkg-source.why: An unencrypted or look-alike source can hand out altered packages.
rule.pkg-source.todo: Point it back at the official registry unless you run that source.
rule.secret.what: A long-lived password or key is stored on this computer
rule.secret.why: Anything that runs as you can copy it. vswarm never reads the value.
rule.secret.todo: Prefer short-lived sign-in; keep production keys in the vault.
rule.vswarm-state.what: vswarm's own records were changed outside vswarm
rule.vswarm-state.why: Someone who can change them could hide what they did.
rule.vswarm-state.todo: If you didn't do it, treat this computer as suspect: vswarm respond.
rule.team-require.what: Your team asks for something this computer doesn't have yet
rule.team-require.why: Your team's policy sets the minimum for production access.
rule.team-require.todo: See what's missing in a terminal: vswarm team status.
rule._action.what: Something that could be an attack
rule._action.why: It matches what attackers do to stay on a computer or steal access.
rule._action.todo: Don't use production until you know what it is. See vswarm diff, or vswarm respond.
rule._yours.why: vswarm points out changes so nothing arrives unseen.
rule._yours.todo: If it's yours, mark it as yours.
